It has been revealed that for orthogonal validation, we leveraged a human CSF proteome dataset from healthy control participants and individuals with AD. Among the significantly differentially abundant proteins (Supplementary Table 7), five corresponded to significant DEGs across main cell types, three in endothelial cells, a primary component of the blood–brain barrier (Extended Data Fig. 6a): increased hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) and decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y. These align with blood–brain barrier dysfunction as an early AD feature32, reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y reflecting loss of neuroprotection33,34 and elevated HPRT suggesting the purine-salvage stress response35. Microglial PGK1 upregulation indicates a glycolytic shift characteristic of pro-inflammatory microglia36,37. PTPRN points to an altered OPC state38. GSEA on microglial DEGs revealed enrichment for G2M checkpoint, mTORC1 signalling and cholesterol homeostasis. These findings suggest that in early AD, microglia may enter a complex, supportive state. The mTORC1 signature points to metabolic reprogramming, and the cholesterol homeostasis signature is consistent with enhanced cholesterol efflux linked to amyloid-β phagocytosis, together suggesting an early supportive microglial response (Fig. 4b).

It has been revealed that because cellular senescence contributes to ageing and neurodegeneration39, we scored three senescence signatures—Canonical senescence, Senescence responses and Senescence initiators (Fig. 4c)—alongside three overlapping NFT signatures39 (Extended Data Fig. 6b–d and Supplementary Table 8), across cell types. Microglia, leukocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells revealed the highest scores, elevated with both ageing (control) and AD (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d), whereas neuronal NFT was most pronounced in the patient with APOE4/4 familial AD (AD_44) (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). These findings suggest a dichotomy: senescence in non-neuronal cells may contribute to microenvironmental dysfunction in AD, whereas neuronal NFTs reflect a distinct, tau-driven pathology that escalates with disease progression or genetic susceptibility. This highlights the potential for different, cell-type-specific therapeutic targets. To ask whether these transcriptomic changes could relate to the subregion volume changes seen by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we examined pathways regulating cell size and tissue architecture. A curated mTOR signalling gene set (core regulators MTOR, RPTOR, RHEB, TSC1/2 and DEPTOR; effectors RPS6KB1, EIF4EBP1 and SREBF1/2) showed an increased module score in AD, most prominently in non-neuronal cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e and Supplementary Table 9). Because mTORC1 regulates cell growth and size40, this raises cellular hypertrophy as one speculative contributor to the volume increases observed at the macrostructural level. Conversely, an extracellular matrix (ECM) gene set (collagens COL1A1 and COL4A1; proteoglycans ACAN, BCAN and VCAN; glycoproteins SPARC,and TNC) showed a decreased module score in AD (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 9). These shifts suggest cell-size regulation and extracellular remodelling as candidate molecular processes potentially relevant to the subregion volume changes.

Microglia are central to brain ageing and neurodegeneration11,41,42. We applied trajectory inference43,44 to microglia from all conditions (young, older control participants and AD), inferring a continuous ageing-to-AD trajectory (Fig. 4d, Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 10). The pseudotime continuum was categorized into four stages: ageing phases of microglia from young participants (stage 1) and older control participants (stage 2), a late ageing phase enriched for older control participants (stage 3, representing a later state for these cells along the trajectory) and AD (stage 4) microglia (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 7a–e). A subset of microglia from older control individuals appeared at earlier trajectory points, whereas some microglia from young individuals persisted into later stages, suggesting that certain microglia may retain youthful properties whereas others show heightened susceptibility to early pathological changes.

We scored three microglial signatures with UCell45 across pseudotime: (1) homeostatic (CSF1R and CX3CR1); (2) stage 1 disease-associated microglia (DAM1) (APOE and B2M), which are typically activated by ageing and amyloid plaques and (3) stage 2 DAM (DAM2) (AXL and CLEC7A), which are dependent on TREM2 signalling46,47. The scores showed a transition from homeostatic towards DAM1 with a modest DAM2 rise (Fig. 4e,f), some of which were validated in the CSF proteomics data (Extended Data Fig. 7f). This observed shift from homeostatic-to-DAM states underscores the critical role of microglial functional changes in AD progression and highlights the potential for therapeutic interventions aimed at preserving homeostatic functions or preventing the full transition to detrimental DAM states.

Moran’s I test identified 13,104 trajectory-associated DEGs (t-DEGs) (Supplementary Table 11 and Extended Data Fig. 7g), smoothed with RVAgene48 and clustered (Fig. 4g). Gene Ontology biological process analysis of these t-DEGs revealed that the ageing phase shifts from cilium assembly and mitochondrial morphogenesis towards stress responses, including amyloid precursor protein catabolic processes, and the disease phase shifts from cell morphogenesis and synaptic modulation to viral response pathways and protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum (Fig. 4h).

According to recent reports, to test generalization beyond our cohort and the hypothalamus, we compared against the PsychAD single-nucleus atlas of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex49,50. AD-associated expression was directionally concordant across non-neuronal cell types and strongest in glia, whereas endothelial cells highlighted more region-specific changes consistent with the distinct vascular microenvironment of the hypothalamus (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 12). In two independent PsychAD cohorts (ageing, 208 donors49; AD, 585 donors)50, DAM signatures rose with age and AD status, recapitulating our homeostatic-to-DAM progression (Extended Data Fig. 8b–g and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these cross-cohort, cross-region comparisons indicate that the main transcriptomic signatures identified in the HypoAD hypothalamus are reproducible in independently generated datasets.

Neurons in the human hypothalamus show extensive cell-type diversity13,21,22. We analysed 213,469 neuronal nuclei, classifying them into three neurotransmitter-defined categories: inhibitory and/or γ-aminobutyric acid-ergic (GABAergic) (GAD2), excitatory and/or glutamatergic (SLC17A6) and histaminergic neurons (HDC) (Fig. 5a–c). Hierarchical Leiden clustering yielded five levels of clustering (5 to 254 subclusters). Anatomical origin was inferred from curated subregional markers21 (Extended Data Fig. 9a), with the dominant subregion listed first for subclusters expressing several markers (Extended Data Fig. 9a). A dendrogram related subtypes across resolutions, with nodes and leaves labelled by distinguishing markers. The 254 leaf subclusters were annotated by relative abundance within the total neuronal population, their distribution across young participants, older control participants and patients with AD, and inferred subregion (Fig. 5d).

In a recent development, a, UMAP of 213,469 hypothalamic neurons, colour-coded by main neurotransmitter category: GABAergic (GAD2-expressing; blue), glutamatergic (SLC17A6-expressing; orange) and histaminergic (HDC-expressing; green). b, Feature plots overlaid on the UMAP, illustrating the normalized expression of GAD2 (GABAergic), SLC17A6 (glutamatergic) and HDC (histaminergic) across the neuronal populations. c, UMAP of neuronal nuclei, coloured by inferred subregional identity on the basis of marker gene expression (colour key in d), highlighting the regional distribution of neuronal clusters within the hypothalamus. d, Circular dendrogram illustrating the relationships among the 254 identified hypothalamic neuron subtypes. For each subtype, the dendrogram is annotated with its inferred subregional identity (on the basis of marker genes) and its relative contribution from young participants, older control participants and patients with AD. e, Significant DEGs identified within the top 30 transcriptionally altered neuronal subtypes. DEGs are grouped by whether the subtype belongs to the GABAergic, glutamatergic or histaminergic category. f, Heatmap showing significantly enriched Reactome pathways within AD-altered GABAergic neurons. g, UMAP showing the 30 neuronal subtypes with the most significant transcriptional changes in early AD. Subtypes are coloured by their inferred hypothalamic subregional origin. h, Heatmap showing significantly enriched Reactome pathways within AD-altered neuronal subtypes. Highlighted pathways include those related to vasopressin-like receptors, GPCR signalling and immune and/or cytokine signalling. AD, patients with AD; CTL, non-AD individuals; GABA, GABAergic; GLU, glutamatergic; HIST, histaminergic; R, subregion annotations; Y, young individuals from ref. 22.

Sources indicate that the hypothalamus comprises distinct neuronal populations with specialized homeostatic roles, yet their subtype-specific contributions to AD remain poorly characterized. To address this, we performed pseudobulk differential gene expression (edgeR LRT) across the 254 neuronal subtypes, prioritizing the top 30 by DEG count, grouped by neurotransmitter category (Fig. 5e). Notably, GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons showed the most pronounced changes, with enriched Reactome pathways for peptide ligand-binding receptors and G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling (Fig. 5f), suggesting a potential dysregulation of neuropeptide signalling and synaptic function in the early-AD hypothalamus that may contribute to metabolic disturbances characteristic of AD pathogenesis.

Sources indicate that the top 30 subtypes were mapped by inferred subregional identity in uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) and spatial locations (Fig. 5g,h, Extended Data Fig. 9b–d and Supplementary Table 14), with other identities validated against the Visium spatial transcriptomics from nine human donors13,51 (Extended Data Fig. 10). This analysis highlighted neurons within the SCN as particularly vulnerable: a prominent SCN cluster (C254-58) revealed altered GPCR and vasopressin-related receptor pathways. Vasopressin, encoded by AVP (Extended Data Fig. 11a), is a key neuropeptide mainly synthesized and secreted by SCN neurons in a circadian manner52 and is crucial for maintaining circadian homeostasis. These findings indicate that early AD disrupts SCN neuronal function, potentially contributing to the circadian dysregulation often observed in patients.

In a recent development, we validated our findings in the PsychAD cohort at the neuronal level, comparing cortical and hypothalamic glutamatergic and GABAergic lineages. AD-associated changes in glutamatergic neurons were more concordant across regions than in GABAergic neurons (Extended Data Fig. 11b and Supplementary Table 15), with cross-region concordance weaker for neurons than for glia, consistent with greater regional specialization of neuronal identity.

We next asked how the molecular signal relates to MRI volume within matched subregions, computing per-modality area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for AD status (amyloid-positive and cognitively impaired versus all others; subregion volume for MRI; pseudobulk PC1 for snRNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 12a–c). The modalities were concordant for some subregions and divergent for others, with no single modality uniformly superior. The SCN was more discriminative transcriptomically than by volume, consistent with its neuronal signatures described above. Imaging and transcriptomics thus provide non-redundant, regionally specific windows into hypothalamic AD pathology and combining them offers a more complete picture than either alone.

Recent findings suggest that for a controlled cross-species comparison, we profiled the hypothalamus in the 5xFAD mouse model. We performed snRNA-seq on hypothalamic tissue from 8-month-old female 5xFAD mice and age-matched wild-type controls (Extended Data Fig. 13), a relatively early stage in the disease progression. The 5xFAD hypothalamus recapitulated the main DAM marker changes and immune response enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 13 and Supplementary Table 16). Neuronal subtypes and subregions were annotated with HypoMap53 (Extended Data Fig. 14). Differential expression analysis (5xFAD versus wild-type) across subregions highlighted alterations in GPCR signalling and ligand–receptor interactions within the SCN, alongside transcriptional changes in the DMH, lateral hypothalamus, ARC and paraventricular nucleus subregions (Extended Data Fig. 14 and Supplementary Table 16).

It has been revealed that together, these analyses reveal selective transcriptional dysregulation in specific hypothalamic neuronal subtypes and subregions in AD, with a particular impact on GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons and the SCN. The pronounced alterations in neuropeptide signalling (for example, vasopressin) and GPCR pathways within the SCN suggest a mechanistic link to circadian rhythm disruption, a hallmark of AD that can precede cognitive decline. These findings position the hypothalamus as a critical, vulnerable hub in AD pathogenesis, advocating for therapeutic strategies that target neuropeptide-GPCR signalling, circadian entrainment or subregion-specific resilience mechanisms to potentially mitigate preclinical AD symptoms.

Sources indicate that our findings provide a multimodal view of how the hypothalamus is altered in ageing and early AD, illustrating region-specific and cell-type-specific changes that have not been observed previously. Neuroimaging studies have suggested that hypothalamic volume correlates with both ageing and cognitive decline, albeit with a relatively small effect size compared with other well-studied vulnerable brain regions54. This relative volumetric stability may reflect the region’s evolutionarily conserved nature and its critical role in survival. Here, by using a recently developed, high-resolution atlas of the human hypothalamus15, we detected specific volumetric changes in 13 distinct hypothalamic subregions that would be masked by more coarse-grained analyses with low-resolution imaging data.

Specifically, we found that although certain nuclei (for example, the lateral hypothalamus) diminish in size with age, others (for example, the SCN and ARC) can show an increase in volume among older adults, even when controlling for amyloid-β pathology and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings suggest that hypothalamic nuclei undergo differential volumetric changes with ageing, even in the absence of AD. However, in comparison to ageing and sex, differences in the volumes of hypothalamic nuclei in the context of amyloid-β deposition and cognitive impairment were more modest or absent. This could be related to lower early AD-related neurodegeneration in the hypothalamus compared with other brain regions or, instead, a poor sensitivity of volumetric analysis in detecting AD-related effects on the hypothalamus with limited sample size. In addition, compared with more vulnerable brain regions such as the hippocampus, the whole hypothalamus and other autonomic regions seem to remain stable with ageing, suggesting potential compensatory mechanisms conferring its resilience as it is evolutionarily conserved and vital for survival55.

To investigate the cellular and molecular effects of AD in individual hypothalamic nuclei, we performed snRNA-seq on post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from control donors and donors with early-stage AD, revealing key molecular features related to the inflammatory response and circadian rhythms that distinguish cells from control donors versus those from donors with AD by machine learning. Further analysis with trajectory inference and differential expression identified striking vulnerabilities in microglia, GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons and specifically circadian rhythm and sleep-regulating neurons predicted to be from SCN and DMH. Consistent with other brain regions, microglia, which are widely recognized mediators of brain ageing and neurodegeneration2,41,42, emerged as particularly prone to transcriptional reprogramming in the hypothalamus in early AD, although our unpaired, cross-sectional data cannot establish a causal or directional relationship.

Sources indicate that the observed alignment of volumetric and molecular vulnerability in the SCN points to the circadian circuitry of the hypothalamus as a potentially vulnerable node in ageing and AD, placing our findings within a broader literature on circadian dysfunction in AD. Circadian disruption, including fragmented sleep–wake cycles, sundowning and altered melatonin secretion, is a well-recognized clinical feature of AD that often precedes cognitive symptoms and may accelerate disease progression8, and the SCN is the central regulator that governs these rhythms. However, because the SCN is among the subregions with lower volumetric reliability (together with mammillary body, dorsal periventricular nucleus and tuberomammillary nucleus), we interpret its volumetric association with particular caution; its involvement in our conclusions rests mainly on the orthogonal molecular evidence. We further note that resolving volume changes in these small nuclei approaches the limits of the 3T MRI-based methods used here; emerging techniques such as ultra-high-field MRI may substantially improve the reliability of subregion volumetry in vivo56. Nevertheless, our study adds converging volumetric and transcriptomic evidence that the SCN and DMH are particularly affected in ageing and AD, through dysregulated vasopressin signalling in SCN neurons, microglial inflammatory remodelling and pronounced vulnerability of GABAergic neurons implicated in circadian regulation.

Returning to the volumetric findings, our molecular data may offer candidate, although speculative, explanations for the subregion volume increases we observed with age and AD. Although these changes are small, the single-cell analyses point to several cellular mechanisms that may underlie them. Main cell-type composition in the 5xFAD whole-hypothalamus mouse data was comparable between early-AD and control animals, consistent with earlier studies with limited sample sizes in humans57,58, suggesting that the observed volumetric effects are unlikely to reflect frank gain or loss of cells, at least at this disease stage. Instead, our data implicate changes in cell size and state: we observed enrichment for ECM remodelling and mTOR signalling, which regulates cell growth, alongside inflammation signatures in non-neuronal cells. A likely contributor is reactive gliosis, which develops in the ageing hypothalamus and can manifest as apparent volume increases on structural MRI even without neuronal loss, as also reported for the hypothalamus in obesity59. Together with previous reports of neuronal hypertrophy in the human hypothalamus with age60, these changes suggest a possible link between cellular remodelling and macrostructural volume. We emphasize, however, that this link is a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: given the large spatial-scale gap between single-nucleus transcriptomic signatures and macroscopic MRI volume, and the transcriptional noise inherent to snRNA-seq, it cannot be inferred from the transcriptomic data alone and would require spatially resolved protein or histological validation. More fundamentally, fully unifying the two modalities remains challenging. Because the volumetric and molecular data derive from separate cohorts without paired, coregistered measurements in the same individuals, we did not attempt coupled statistical integration, such as multimodal embedding or the prediction of molecular state from imaging features. Instead, we compared the AD-predictive signal of each modality at matched anatomical subregions, revealing that imaging and transcriptomics provide non-redundant and regionally specific windows into hypothalamic pathology (Extended Data Fig. 12a–c). True integration, in which volumetric and molecular features are jointly modelled in a shared statistical framework, will require future studies that acquire both modalities from the same individuals, ideally with spatially coregistered sampling.

In summary, our combined volumetric and single-cell atlas of the human hypothalamus provides a high-resolution framework for elucidating how ageing and AD pathology differentially affect specific hypothalamic subregions and cell types. We highlight notable vulnerabilities in GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons, SCN and DMH circadian regulators, and inflammatory microglial cascades, underscoring their potential roles in instigating early hypothalamic dysfunction.

The brain MRI scans used in this study were obtained from two separate datasets. The first was from the AMBR study16. A second dataset from the CBA study17 was added to improve rigour and reproducibility. Both studies obtained 0.8-mm isotropic T1 magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo and T2 sampling perfection with application-optimized contrasts using different flip-angle evolution sequences for segmentation and volumetric analysis of specific hypothalamic nuclei as described in ref. 15. Although several other high-resolution brain MRI datasets exist, the AMBR and CBA studies also obtained assessments of brain amyloid-β deposition and cognitive impairment. Differences in other aspects of the AMBR and CBA studies, such as cohort characteristics, were seen as valuable to improve the robustness and generalizability of this study. Test–retest reliability of the segmentation pipeline was assessed using the ICC ((2,1); two-way random effects, absolute agreement, single measurement) in eight participants with repeat scans in the CBA study. Following ref. 61, we classified ICC < 0.40 as poor and 0.40–0.59 as fair; we note that other schemes, such as ref. 62, place the poor–moderate boundary at 0.50. For structures with poor ICC, we later corroborate the volumetric findings with a complementary molecular modality. All associations reported here are based on bilateral (combined left and right) volumes; hemisphere-specific measures, which are inherently noisier, were examined only descriptively and did not form the basis of our conclusions.

To specifically assess the effect of AD on subregion volumes, participants were categorized on the basis of their amyloid-β and cognitive status. Amyloid status was determined from amyloid positron emission tomography imaging or CSF biomarker assessments when available using study-specific criteria: in AMBR, labelling was based on Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (ADRC) cut-offs for [carbon-11]-Pittsburgh compound B (C-11 PiB) standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), [fluorine-18]-florbetapir (F-18 AV-45) SUVR, by visual read when SUVR data were not available, or by CSF test results. In the CBA study, labelling was based on provided centiloid values thresholded at 16.4, corresponding to the Knight ADRC C-11 PiB mean cortical SUVR cut-off of 1.42 (ref. 63). If amyloid-β status was positive any time before or up to 1 year after the MRI, it was labelled as positive. Conversely if amyloid-β status was negative any time after or up to 1  year before the MRI, it was labelled as negative. Otherwise amyloid-β status was considered not available (NA).

Cognitive status was labelled as ‘impaired’ or ‘unimpaired’ using study-specific criteria. In the AMBR study, labelling was based on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale (CDR), with CDR = 0 indicating cognitively unimpaired and CDR > 0 indicating cognitive impairment. A subject was labelled as impaired only if assessed as impaired within ±1 year of the MRI, and as unimpaired only if assessed as unimpaired at any time after the MRI or within 1 year before (otherwise coded as NA). In the CBA study, labelling was based on the timepoint-specific diagnosis code, with code 1 indicating cognitively unimpaired; codes 2, 4, 5 and 6 indicating evidence of cognitive impairment and code 3 (subjective impairment) coded as NA.

Sources indicate that in both studies, individuals meeting criteria for both cognitive impairment and positive amyloid-β status were designated as the AD group. Conversely, participants without cognitive deficits and with negative amyloid-β status were classified as the non-AD (control) group. To minimize potential confounding from intermediate pathology profiles, only individuals clearly falling into these AD or non-AD categories were included in these specific comparative analyses. The cohort had a mean age of 63.4 ± 11.6 years (mean ± standard deviation) and included 60.5% women. Moreover, our dataset includes information directly relevant to AD, including 30.6% with abnormal cognitive status and 13.8% who were amyloid-β positive (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The mean total hypothalamic volume for this cohort was 736.2 ± 88.2 mm3.

Given that the dataset did not have predefined group structures for all desired comparisons, we used a GLM to assess the associations between hypothalamic subregion volumes (summed across left and right hemispheres) and various demographic and clinical variables.

Specifically, in the AMBR study (n = 202), we modelled (denoted as ‘~’) the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume (log[subregion volume]) as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive (cogn.) status, amyloid-β deposition status and other relevant covariates, where ‘+’ denotes additive main effects, ‘:’ denotes an interaction, ‘×’ denotes crossed terms (main effects plus their interaction), and ‘scale()’ denotes z-score standardization of a covariate:.

P values for individual variables from the GLM analyses were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR).

In the CBA study (n = 256), the metabolic and sleep covariates (body mass index (BMI)), HgbA1c and Epworth Sleepiness Score) were not available; we therefore modelled the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume (log[subregion volume]) as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive status, amyloid-β deposition status, their interaction and ICV:.

In the harmonized two-study pooled cohort (AMBR + CBA, n = 458), we modelled the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive status, amyloid-β deposition status, their interaction, ICV and study of origin. The metabolic and sleep covariates above were not included here as they were not available across both studies:.

To test whether the association between age and subregion volume differed by disease status, we fitted a separate GLM that included an age × group interaction term, where group distinguished cognitively normal, amyloid-negative individuals from all others:.

Recent findings suggest that to compare subregion volumes between patients with AD and non-AD individuals while balancing demographic differences, we constructed a logistic regression model to estimate each participant’s propensity score for AD-group membership, using sex and age at MRI as covariates. Propensity-score matching was then performed using a nearest-neighbour algorithm, generating matched pairs of patients with AD and non-AD individuals with similar distributions of sex and age. This balanced these key covariates between groups for the subsequent volumetric comparisons.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the predictive power of hypothalamic volumes in identifying AD and cognitive status, we conducted a series of binary classification tasks using receiver-operating-characteristic analysis. Three primary target conditions were defined: (1) cognitive status (impaired ‘A’ versus normal ‘N’), (2) amyloid status (positive ‘P’ versus negative ‘N’) and (3) a composite AD group (A+P+ versus all others). For each condition, we compared the diagnostic performance of two distinct feature sets: a multivariate model comprising 13 individual hypothalamic subregions (ARC, anterior hypothalamic area, dorsal periventricular nucleus, DMH, lateral hypothalamus, medial preoptic nucleusMPO, paraventricular nucleus, posterior hypothalamus, periventricular nucleus, SCN, supraoptic nucleus, tuberomammillary nucleus, ventromedial nucleus) and a univariate model using only the total hypothalamic volume. Classification was performed using logistic regression with balanced class weights to account for potential group size discrepancies. Model performance was validated using a fivefold stratified cross-validation approach. Features were standardized (z-score normalized) within each training fold before model fitting. The resulting area under the curve was calculated as the mean across cross-validation folds, with the standard deviation reported as a measure of model stability.

Given the central role of the hypothalamus in energy homeostasis and metabolic regulation, we examined whether BMI was associated with hypothalamic volume at the total and subregion level. BMI was not significantly associated with total hypothalamic volume (estimate ± s.e. = −0.005 ± 0.007, adjusted P = 0.505, Extended Data Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 4) or with any bilateral subregion volume after FDR correction (all adjusted P > 0.086). In lateralized analyses, the left DMH showed a significant negative association with BMI (left DMH −0.042 ± 0.014, adjusted P = 0.014), although this was not observed on the right side (right DMH −0.010 ± 0.018, adjusted P = 0.664, Extended Data Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 4).

Recent findings suggest that unfixed, flash-frozen half-hypothalamus tissues were obtained from the Netherlands Brain Bank (NBB), Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience, Amsterdam (open access at www.brainbank.nl). All material has been collected from donors for or from whom a written informed consent for a brain autopsy and the use of the material and clinical information for research purposes had been obtained by the NBB.

This consent procedure was approved by the Ethical Committee of the VU University Medical Center (Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, the Netherlands), independently and before this study. Tissue blocks were stored at −80 °C.

Industry observers note that the cohort comprised 14 donors: 7 control participants without dementia and 7 patients with AD (6 sporadic and 1 familial). Comorbidities were common in both groups and predominantly cardiovascular; control participants also included donors with malignancy (colorectal carcinoma, multiple myeloma, melanoma), whereas the AD group included one donor each with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and bladder carcinoma. Causes of death included acute cardiac events and pulmonary embolism (control participants), euthanasia (2 control participants), end-stage malignancy (control participants) and respiratory insufficiency, aspiration pneumonia, cachexia, ileus and dehydration due to swallowing problems (AD patients). No donor had a documented intensive care unit admission; all deaths occurred in community, nursing home or palliative care settings. All key determinants of post-mortem gene expression quality (age, post-mortem interval, brain pH, RNA integrity number and agonal state estimated from clinical records) were comparable between groups (all P > 0.1 with Mann–Whitney U test). All samples showed high quality, with short post-mortem intervals of less than 9 h and RNA integrity number scores above 6.5. Full donor-level clinical and neuropathological details can be requested from the NBB using the NBB ID, which is available on request.

It has been revealed that to overcome the input cell number limits of droplet-based single-cell sequencing (which typically captures tens of thousands of cells per sample) relative to the vast cellularity of the entire hypothalamus, we performed targeted macrodissection. In this initial study, we prioritized in-depth profiling of three subregions already implicated in ageing and AD over a shallower survey of the whole hypothalamus: the ARC, a hub for energy homeostasis housing pro-opiomelanocortin and agouti-related peptide neurons that integrate leptin and insulin signals64,65; the SCN, the master circadian pacemaker whose disruption underlies sleep–wake disturbances among the earliest non-cognitive symptoms of AD66,67; and the mammillary nucleus, a component of the Papez memory circuit disproportionately vulnerable to neurodegeneration in AD models10. Together, these subregions span the anterior–posterior extent of the hypothalamus and represent three of its main functional domains: metabolic control, circadian regulation, and memory circuitry. Focusing on three primary regions of interest, the ARC, SCN and mammillary nucleus, prevented the severe dilution of rare neuronal populations, ensuring sufficient sampling depth for downstream differential expression analysis. Macrodissection was performed on hemisected hypothalami within a Leica cryostat at the lowest temperature setting, with the tissue surrounded by dry ice. To maintain RNA integrity and prevent cross-contamination, the blade and all dissection tools were sanitized and treated with RNaseZap RNase Decontamination Solution between each sample.

Industry observers note that wild-type and heterozygous (8-month-old) 5xFAD-C57BL/6 female mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory. Mice were housed and used according to protocols approved by Brown University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and in accordance with institutional and national guidelines. Animals were housed at 21 ± 1 °C (70 ± 2 °F) with humidity from 50% to 70%. Animals were fed ad libitum Lab Diet 5010 chow and water. The light cycle was 12 h on 12 h off and lights were on between 7:00 and 19:00. Animals were exposed to male bedding 3 d before being euthanized to synchronize the oestrous cycle. Animals were euthanized at Zeitgeber time ZT2–ZT3. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Animals were not randomly allocated to experimental groups. Investigators were not blinded to group allocation during the experiments or outcome assessment.

It has been revealed that no statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes, but our donor numbers are comparable to those of established snRNA-seq studies of the human brain in AD, which typically profiled 3–10 donors per group68,69,70. Individual nuclei were excluded from analysis on the basis of quality control metrics (feature count and mitochondrial read count). Data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

Industry observers note that nuclei extraction was performed using the Nuclei PURE Prep kit (Millipore Sigma) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All procedures were performed in the cold room before the 45-min spin down. Tissue was transferred using a transfer pipette into a refrigerated Dounce homogenizer with 5 ml of lysis solution following kit instructions. Tissue was homogenized with the Dounce B and the lysate was transferred into a 15-ml Falcon tube through a 40-μm filter. The sucrose purification step was performed with the modifications that half the volume of all reagents was used to account for the small tissue sample sizes, an SW34 rotor was used and samples were spun for 45 min at 30,000g (13,000 r.p.m.) at 4 °C.

It has been revealed that nuclei were counted using a hemocytometer and 10,000 nuclei per sample were loaded onto the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Chip (10x Genomics) and processed with the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics). Samples were sequenced at GENEWIZ on an Illumina NovaSeq, with a target of 50,000 reads per sample.

Sequence alignment for human snRNA-seq data (including the dataset from ref. 22) was performed against the GRCh38 (2020) reference genome. These alignments were executed using Cell Ranger (10x Genomics; v.7.1.0 for human) with the --include-introns flag, essential for capturing nuclear RNA.

Following alignment, systematic background noise, such as ambient RNA, was removed from the count matrices using CellBender (v.0.3.0)71. For quality control, outlier cells were identified on the basis of established criteria. Specifically, cells were flagged as outliers if they exceeded 5 median absolute deviations for any of the following quality control metrics: log1p_total_counts, log1p_n_genes_by_counts or pct_counts_in_top_20_genes. In addition, cells with a mitochondrial transcript percentage of 10% or more were excluded.

According to recent reports, potential doublets (two or more cells captured as a single droplet) were then identified and filtered out using scDblFinder72. After these quality control steps, data from different individuals were integrated using single-cell variational inference23 to correct for batch effects. Subsequent data visualization and downstream analyses were performed using tools from the Seurat73 and Scanpy74 ecosystems.

Subregional samples were never pooled. Each donor contributed three tissue samples obtained by macrodissection enriching for distinct hypothalamic subregions (ARC, SCN, MN), yielding 42 samples across the 14 older donors. Each sample was collected into a separate tube and processed through an independent 10x Chromium channel, producing independent library preparations and therefore constituting a biologically and technically independent observation capturing distinct cellular compositions and independent sources of technical variation.

In a recent development, differential expression analysis was performed using a pseudobulk approach with the LRT in edgeR75. Genes were significant if the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P value was below 0.05. The three young reference donors22 were included only to anchor cell-type annotation and the microglial ageing trajectory; all AD-versus-control differentially expression analysis was restricted to the HypoAD cohort, excluding the familial AD (AD_44) donor.

GSEA was performed using the fgsea package76 with the hallmark gene-set lists and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Reactome gene-set list from Molecular Signatures Database76,77. For GSEA input, genes within each cluster were ranked by their log2 fold change (log2[FC]) values, determined from edgeR LRT differentially expressed analysis. The GSEA was then performed using the fgseaMultilevel() command with default settings. Gene sets were considered significantly enriched if the adjusted P < 0.1.

Sources indicate that to contextualize our data within a broader reference, we used a universal cell embedding (UCE) foundation model. UCE projects single-cell gene expression profiles into a universal embedding space that is agnostic to technical covariates such as batch effects or protocol differences78. We implemented the 33-layer version of UCE as specified in its official repository (https://github.com/snap-stanford/UCE), using Python (v.3.9.0) and PyTorch (v.2.1.1), with the publicly available pretrained model weights.

According to recent reports, we then used UCE to project our control and AD snRNA-seq datasets into a shared embedding space alongside a publicly available, community-curated human brain atlas containing more than 25 million cells78. The resulting embeddings were visualized in a two-dimensional UMAP space to benchmark our newly generated data against this large-scale public reference.

To identify predictive features for the classification task distinguishing cells from AD versus control individuals, we developed and applied a machine learning pipeline using Python (v.3.10.9) and the scikit-learn library (v.1.6.1). The full pipeline is available through GitHub (https://github.com/Webb-Laboratory/HypoAD).

For cell-type-specific models, the full dataset was filtered to include only cells corresponding to a single target cell type (for example, Neuron, Astrocyte), on the basis of predefined annotations.

We used a leave-one-batch-out nested cross-validation strategy to ensure robust hyperparameter tuning, prevent data leakage and give an unbiased performance evaluation. For each of the seven outer folds, an inner sixfold cross-validation was used to tune the model’s hyperparameters. This approach generated seven distinct models, from which we ranked gene-associated weights to identify the most predictive features (Fig. 3a). Specifically, the data for all cells, as well as for each of the top five most abundant cell types, were split into seven outer folds on the basis of the sample batch of origin (leave-one-batch-out). Each batch comprised two donors (one control and one AD), and no donor appeared in more than one batch. For each outer fold, the test set consisted of nuclei from a single held-out batch, such that both donors in that batch were entirely unseen during training. The remaining six batches were used for an inner leave-one-batch-out cross-validation to select the optimal hyperparameters for an Elastic Net logistic regression model. The 5 × 5 hyperparameter grid included a logarithmic search for the regularization parameter C (from 10−2 to 102) and a linear search for the L1 ratio (from 0 to 1). The model with the best average inner-fold AUROC was then retrained on all six training batches and evaluated on the held-out test batch. We first trained a model on all cells, which achieved predictive performance (average AUROC = 0.75). We then trained models specific to the five most abundant cell types. All cell-type-specific models also performed well, with the microglia model showing the highest accuracy (average AUROC = 0.91). The comparatively lower performance for neuronal models may be attributable to the complexity and heterogeneity of neurons in the hypothalamus (Fig. 3b).

According to recent reports, after completing the outer cross-validation, we extracted the feature weights (coefficients) from the seven models, each trained on one outer fold. Two feature ranking lists were generated for each cell type. The ‘raw-weight’ rank was created by ranking all features on the basis of their mean weight across the seven folds, preserving the sign to indicate positive or negative prediction association. The ‘absolute-weight’ rank was created by ranking features on the basis of the mean of their absolute weights to measure overall predictive importance regardless of direction.

Recent findings suggest that to identify features consistently important across all cell types, we defined a ‘shared score’ for each gene as the mean of its absolute-weight rank across the five cell types analysed, and coloured by its direction (that is, whether the feature is on the top or bottom of the raw-weight rank list). Cell-type-specific ranks for features were defined by inquiry_rank/mean_rank_others.

In a recent development, to identify biological pathways associated with our model’s predictions, we performed preranked GSEA using the gseapy (v.1.1.9) Python package. For each cell type, the full list of features was ranked using the mean raw weight. This ranked list was tested for enrichment against the KEGG pathway database (v.2021), Hallmark (v.2020) and Gene Ontology Biological Process (2021) from the Molecular Signatures Database. Significance was determined using a permutation-based test (1,000 permutations), and pathways with FDR q < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

To infer the ageing process for the microglia cluster (n = 51,420 nuclei) generated in Seurat, we applied Monocle3 (refs. 43,44). Monocle3 typically uses dimensionality reduction to position cells in a lower-dimensional space, can correct for batch effects using mutual nearest-neighbour alignment and subsequently connects cells to construct trajectories in a semi-supervised manner.

For our analysis of the microglia–macrophage cluster, we directly used the integrated Seurat object, bypassing any further batch correction or dimensionality reduction steps within Monocle3 itself, as these had been addressed in the previous Seurat processing. After subsetting the microglia cluster, the root of the trajectory was programmatically defined by selecting the principal graph node most enriched for cells originating from young individuals. The horizontal axis in Fig. 4e represents a data-driven transcriptomic pseudotime learned from the single-cell data, not a chronological timeline, and individual donors do not necessarily follow this ordering. Trajectory-based expression analysis along this inferred trajectory was then performed using Moran’s I test, as implemented in Monocle3. Genes with a q value (FDR-adjusted P value) of less than 0.01 were considered significantly trajectory dependent, resulting in the identification of 13,104 such genes.

Functional enrichment analysis of the 13,104 t-DEGs, grouped into individual expression groups identified through co-expression analysis, was performed using Enrichr (v.3.0)79. This analysis used the GO_Biological_Process_2018 gene-set database. Statistically significantly enriched Gene Ontology terms were identified on the basis of a Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P value (Padj) < 0.01. For visualization purposes, the top ten significantly enriched terms per group were shown in a dot plot.

Sources indicate that to decode and visualize the dynamic expression patterns of the t-DEGs (n = 13,104) along the inferred pseudotime trajectory, we used the RVAgene package (v.1.0)48 in Python (v.3.9.6) with PyTorch (v.1.9.0). Before input into RVAgene, expression values for each gene were averaged within discrete pseudotime bins and subsequently rescaled to a range of [−1, 1]. The RVAgene neural network was configured with a symmetrical architecture comprising two hidden layers (48 nodes per layer) and two latent variable dimensions. The smoothed, reconstructed expression trajectories of the t-DEGs generated by RVAgene were then used to create the summary heatmap.

Recent findings suggest that two gene sets were assembled to score mTOR(PI3K-AKT-mTOR) signalling and ECM (matrisome) activity. Each set began from a curated list of canonical genes: for mTOR, core pathway components and downstream lipid–sterol effectors; for ECM, matrisome constituents, including collagens, laminins, proteoglycans, matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors (MMPs or TIMPs) and ADAMTS proteases. Each seed list was expanded by gene-symbol pattern matching (for example, COL[0–9] + A[0–9], MMP[0–9], LAM[ABC][0–9]) and filtered to remove unrelated ‘look-alike’ families (for example, mitochondrial import genes TIMM/TOMM, TIMELESS), then restricted to genes detected in the dataset, yielding 70 mTOR and 157 ECM genes (Supplementary Table 9, tabs mTOR_set and ECM_set).

According to recent reports, counts were normalized with Seurat’s NormalizeData (log-normalization, scale factor 10,000). Per-cell module scores were computed with Seurat’s AddModuleScore (default parameters: 24 expression bins, control pools of 100 randomly sampled genes per set gene), which subtracts the mean expression of a randomly selected control gene set from the mean expression of the target set. mTOR and ECM scores were calculated jointly (Score1 = mTOR, Score2 = ECM). For statistical testing, donors were grouped as young, control or AD. To avoid pseudoreplication, per-cell scores were aggregated to the sample level by taking the mean score across all cells of a given cell type within each sample, retaining only sample × cell-type combinations with ten or more cells. For each cell type and gene set, module scores were compared between control and AD samples using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons across all cell type × gene-set tests using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Analyses were performed in R with Seurat and rstatix.

Recent findings suggest that cell2location is a Bayesian model that uses snRNA-seq cell-type signatures to infer cell types in Visium spatial transcriptomics by decomposing messenger RNA counts in each Visium voxel into cell types. We performed the three main steps in the cell2location workflow: estimating reference expression signatures of cell types using our dataset, mapping the learned cell-type signatures onto the slides, and performing downstream analysis. The code, model parameters and training evaluations can be found in the Jupyter notebooks in our GitHub repository. In brief, we used the default parameters to train the cell2location model.

Lumbar CSF samples from a cohort of 280 participants (including healthy control, AD and other conditions) were analysed by means of liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Samples were processed on a Thermo EASY-nLC 1200 system coupled to a Thermo Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer. Detailed chromatography and data acquisition parameters follow the methods described in ref. 80. Quality control was maintained using inter-batch and inter-experiment samples across 96-well plates to evaluate and correct for technical effects. Protein quantification was performed by mapping raw spectra to an empirically corrected Prosit81 library (generated by means of gas-phase fractionated, narrow-window injections) using EncyclopeDIA, with peak integration and protein mapping finalized in Skyline.

Sources indicate that differential abundance analysis was performed to compare patients with AD (n = 19) against the healthy control group (n = 205) using the limma and eBayes framework82 on the preprocessed and log2 normalized protein quantification table in R. Statistical significance for differential protein abundance was defined by Padj < 0.05.

To validate cell-type-specific transcriptomic signatures at the protein level, significant CSF proteins were intersected with significant DEGs from single-cell pseudobulk analysis (Padj < 0.05). To address nomenclature inconsistencies between modalities, a ‘fuzzy-join’ logic was implemented. This approach matched protein symbols to RNA symbols on the basis of exact matches, prefix alignment and antisense transcript identification.

In a recent development, validation of nine ageing-related and AD-related markers from the microglia pseudotime analysis (CSF1R, CX3CR1, P2RY12, APOE, B2M, CTSB, AXL, CLEC7A and TIMP2 in Fig. 4f) was performed by extracting their corresponding features from the CSF proteomics expression matrix using case-insensitive substring matching. To isolate age-related versus disease-related protein trajectories, the healthy control cohort was further stratified into ‘young’ (less than 65 years of age) and ‘aged’ (65 years or older) subgroups and visualized accordingly. Statistical analysis did not show significant differences between the groups, despite the protein trajectories’ showing trends similar to the gene expression data.

Sources indicate that AD-associated transcriptomic signatures were validated against the PsychAD Consortium single-nucleus RNA-seq resource of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Mount Sinai Brain Bank cohort), obtained from CELLxGENE Discover (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/collections/84ce6837-548d-4a1f-919f-0bc0d9a3952f). Two releases were used: an AD-enriched cohort for disease comparisons and a neurologically normal cohort spanning adulthood for the ageing analysis. For all analyses, Ensembl gene IDs were mapped to HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee symbols using the feature_name field supplied with the dataset, and raw counts were normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and log1p-transformed.

Sources indicate that for cross-cohort differential expression concordance, PsychAD cell types were mapped to their HypoAD counterparts at the main cell-type level. Non-neuronal populations (astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and endothelial cells) were assigned direct one-to-one correspondences. Because neuronal subtypes are largely region-specific and the cortical subtypes annotated in PsychAD do not correspond one-to-one to hypothalamic populations, the finer PsychAD neuronal subtypes were aggregated into glutamatergic and GABAergic (GABA) lineages; for each gene, the subtype result with the lowest FDR was taken as the representative statistic for the lineage. Pseudobulk differential expression (AD versus control) was computed per cell type with edgeR and compared across datasets by plotting the paired log2[FC] of shared genes. Directional concordance of AD-associated changes was quantified with Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ) on the subset of genes significantly differentially expressed (FDR < 0.05) in both datasets.

Recent findings suggest that for microglial DAM module scoring, module scores for homeostatic microglia (HEXB, CST3, CX3CR1, CSF1R, CTSS, TMSB4X, P2RY12, C1QB), DAM1 (TYROBP, CTSB, APOE, B2M, FTH1, TREM2) and DAM2 (TREM2, AXL, CST7, CTSL, LPL, CD9, CSF1, ITGAX, CLEC7A, LILRB4, TIMP2) were computed with scanpy.tl.score_genes (analogous to Seurat’s AddModuleScore). In the ageing cohort, scores were averaged per donor and then per age bin, correlated with age by Spearman’s ρ and shown with locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (bandwidth 0.6); individual representative genes were shown as scatter plots against donor age (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing bandwidth 0.5) and as violin plots comparing donors less than 65 years of age versus those 65 years of age or older. In the AD cohort, the same gene-level visualizations were produced across the four donor groups (young, control, AD and familial AD).

All participants provided written informed consent to participate17. All procedures and research protocols for post-mortem tissue were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Brown University. All research was performed in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Informed consent for the use of post-mortem tissue was obtained from all donors or their next of kin.

I.D. provided guidance on tissue dissection and sample selection. K.R.B. and K.H.H. assisted with tissue processing. A.C.J. contributed to cell-type annotation. M.J.M. provided guidance on validation with quantitative proteomics data. W.S.N. provided guidance on machine learning and interpretation. M.S.G. and A.G.V. provided the MRI dataset and guided the volumetric analysis. D.Y. and A.E.W. wrote the paper, with all authors providing critical feedback.

a, Characteristics of the two studies. b, Test–retest ICC(2,1) for bilateral, left and right regional volumes (two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measurement). Points are ICC estimates. Bars show 95% confidence intervals computed by irr::icc. n = 8 independent participants, each scanned twice (16 scans, paired measurements). Red indicates ICC < 0.4. c, Pearson correlation heatmap of hypothalamic structure volumes and age at MRI in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants (n = 165 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across all pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). d, Age–volume Pearson r in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants, analysed as pooled (black, n = 165), CBA (orange, n = 91) and AMBR (blue, n = 74) samples. Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across 26 age–volume correlations per analysis. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05, open circles non-significance. e, Associations of age, female sex and intracranial volume with subregion volumes in AMBR, CBA and pooled participants. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients. Bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × s.e.). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in pooled models. Two-sided t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. BH correction covered 26 regions per predictor and cohort. Exact estimates, intervals, t statistics, degrees of freedom and raw/adjusted P are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of extrahypothalamic volumes and age at MRI (n = 458 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across unique pairwise correlations within the matrix (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson correlations in the pooled cohort (n = 458 independent participants), CBA (n = 256) and AMBR (n = 202). Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across all 26 regional age–volume correlations within each cohort. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05. Open circles indicate adjusted P ≥ 0.05. c, Forest plots of Gaussian GLM coefficients for hypothalamic (top) and extrahypothalamic (bottom) volumes, ordered by coefficient estimate. Points show fitted coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 316 independent participants in every model, with covariates as in Fig. 1c. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 308 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all eight coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Point color and size indicate adjusted significance. d, Age, female sex and intracranial volume coefficients for extrahypothalamic structures. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in the pooled analysis. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. P values were BH-adjusted across 26 regions separately for each predictor and cohort. e, Body mass index (BMI) associations in AMBR-only Gaussian GLMs. Points show BMI coefficients per SD of BMI and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 174 independent participants in each regional model. Models adjusted for age, sex, cognition, amyloid status, cognition × amyloid status, HbA1c, Epworth sleepiness score and intracranial volume. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 164 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all ten model coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Exact results for all panels are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

Industry observers note that a, PCA of 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structure volumes (n = 458 participants). Scatter plots are colored by eight covariates: age, sex, amyloid-β status, cognitive status, intracranial volume (ICV), total brain volume (TBV), study and amyloid days. Three variants are shown: raw volumes (top, PC1 = 44.2%, PC2 = 14.4%), fully residualized for age, sex, ICV, TBV and study (middle, PC1 = 27.6%, PC2 = 13.1%), and partially residualized for sex, ICV, TBV and study (bottom, PC1 = 27.4%, PC2 = 13.9%). b–c, PC1 and PC2 loadings from raw (b) and fully residualized (c) PCA. Bars are red for negative loadings and teal for positive loadings. d, Changes in PC1 (left) and PC2 (right) loadings from raw (orange) to fully residualized (green) PCA, shown as dumbbell plots ordered by magnitude of change. e, Associations of PC1–PC5 scores with nine covariates in raw and partially residualized PCA. Continuous covariates were tested using two-sided Pearson correlations, with r2 as effect size. Categorical covariates were tested using omnibus one-way ANOVA F-tests, with η2 as effect size and an upper-tail F reference distribution. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted across 45 PC–covariate tests separately for each PCA variant. n = 458 participants, with data available for cognitive status in 422, amyloid-β status in 340, CogDays in 441 and AmyloidDays in 358. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. f, Regional volume versus age in n = 181 independent male participants. Each point represents one participant, colored by combined cognitive and amyloid status (black, missing status). Black LOESS curves estimate conditional mean volume. Shading reveals pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the fitted curves, rather than between-participant standard deviations. g, Regional volume distributions after nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching of AD and cognitively unimpaired, amyloid-negative participants on sex and age. The pooled comparison includes 24 AD participants (18 men, 6 women) and 24 matched controls (16 men, 8 women). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Dots represent individual participants, including observations beyond the whiskers. Duplicate outlier symbols are suppressed. h, ROC curves from class-balanced logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation, using 13 hypothalamic subregion volumes or total hypothalamic volume to predict cognitive impairment (n = 422 participants, 140 impaired, 282 unimpaired), amyloid positivity (n = 340, 63 positive, 277 negative) and AD status (n = 316, 24 AD, 292 others). AUCs are mean ± standard deviation across five folds. The subregion model had a higher mean AUC for all three outcomes. No formal comparison was performed. i, Univariate ROC curves predicting AD status from 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures and total hypothalamic volume (n = 316 participants, 24 AD, 292 others), sorted by descending AUC. The arcuate nucleus (AN; ARC in the main text), fornix (fx), paraventricular nucleus (Pa) and ventromedial nucleus (VM) were the strongest predictors. When lower volume predicted AD (indicated by “−”), scores were sign-inverted before ROC calculation.

a, Split UMAP embeddings of hypothalamic microglia/macrophage nuclei by group: young, 3,213 nuclei (3 donors), CTL, 24,648 (7 donors), AD, 20,087 (6 donors), and AD_44, 3,472 (1 donor), totaling 51,420 nuclei. In each panel, the full population is shown in light gray and the indicated group is overlaid, colored by inferred pseudotime (top), group identity (middle) or local nuclear density (2D kernel density estimate, bottom). Young nuclei occupy a discrete low-pseudotime region, whereas AD nuclei are shifted toward high pseudotime. b, Group-specific kernel density estimates of pseudotime, with the pooled distribution shown in gray. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Dashed vertical lines mark mean pseudotime: young 1.50, CTL 2.38, AD 2.90 and AD_44 2.12. The distribution shifts rightward from young to CTL to AD. c, Empirical cumulative distributions of nuclear pseudotime. The maximal vertical separation between AD and CTL is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance D = 0.27, presented as a descriptive effect size. Because nuclei within a donor are not independent, inference used donor-level mean pseudotime: AD versus CTL, 6 versus 7 donors, two-sided exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.0047. Young and AD_44 are shown descriptively and were not tested. d, Group composition of 22 fixed-width pseudotime bins (width 0.2, early to late from left to right). Each bar shows the fraction of nuclei contributed by each group. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and were not tested. The AD fraction increases along pseudotime (Spearman ρ = 0.97, n = 22 bins, two-sided unadjusted P = 1.0 × 10−13), from near-absence in the earliest bins to dominance in the latest bins. A donor-aware binomial mixed model (in-segment versus out, group + (1 | donor), two-sided Wald tests, BH-adjusted across 44 segment × comparison tests) showed AD nuclei were underrepresented relative to CTL in early bins 4–9 (log-OR − 3.23 to −1.28, adjusted P ≤ 0.017) and overrepresented in late bins 16–21 (log-OR +0.62 to +1.31, adjusted P ≤ 0.044), with a single crossover at pseudotime ≈ 2.3–2.9. Exact estimates for every bin are in Supplementary Table 10. e, Nuclear pseudotime by group, with counts as in a. Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Nuclei beyond the whiskers are plotted individually. This panel is descriptive. See c for donor-level inference. f, Top: per-nucleus expression of CSF1R, APOE, B2M and TIMP2 in microglia (same data as Fig. 4f). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Asterisks indicate FDRs from pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests (AD versus CTL, 1 d.f., one pseudobulk per sample, 18 AD samples from 6 donors and 21 CTL samples from 7 donors, BH-adjusted across genes): CSF1R FDR = 3.1 × 10−7 (****). APOE, B2M and TIMP2 were nonsignificant (FDR ≥ 0.05). Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and excluded from these tests. Bottom: CSF protein abundance in young healthy controls (<65 years, n = 38 participants), aged healthy controls (≥65 years, n = 167) and AD (n = 19). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Each dot represents one participant. g, Embeddings of microglial trajectory-associated genes, colored by trajectory rank (left) or correlation with AD status (right).

Oligodendrocytes ρ = 0.894, n = 191, P = 1.2 × 10−67. OPCs ρ = 0.978, n = 17, P = 6.1 × 10−6. Endothelial cells ρ = −0.667, n = 8, P = 0.083. Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. a, Ranked bar charts of univariate AUROC for distinguishing AD status using neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores (top) and MRI-derived volumetric measures (bottom). MRI participant counts are as in b. b, Cross-modal comparison of univariate AUROC between MRI-derived volume and neuronal snRNA-seq pseudobulk PC1 scores for matched hypothalamic regions (1:1 pairing). Left: snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC, with a dashed line indicating equal performance. Right: AUROC estimates for each modality by region, with lines connecting matched estimates. Each dot represents one AUROC estimate, not a biological replicate. No error bars or cross-modal tests are shown. Score direction was chosen so that AUROC ≥ 0.5. The dashed vertical line indicates chance (AUROC = 0.5). MRI AUROCs used 316 participants: 24 with AD, defined as cognitively impaired and amyloid-β positive, and 292 without AD. snRNA-seq AUROCs used donor-level pseudobulks from 14 biologically independent donors (7 AD, 7 control) for ARC, PVH, SCN, MN, PO, TM, ZI and the whole hypothalamus, 13 donors (7 AD, 6 control) for LH, and 10 donors (5 AD, 5 control) for VMH and DMH. c, Cross-modal comparison as in b, with snRNA-seq AUROC averaged across neuronal subregion annotations containing the matched region. For example, AN includes ARC, ARC_SCN, ARC_SMN, LH_ARC, PO_ARC, SCN_ARC, VMH_ARC and ZI_ARC. Left: mean snRNA-seq AUROC versus MRI AUROC. Right: bars show MRI AUROC and mean snRNA-seq AUROC, and dots show individual annotation AUROCs. Error bars show sample standard deviations (n − 1 denominator) across annotations and appear only when at least three annotations match. Matching annotation counts are 8 (AN/ARC), 6 (Pa/PVH), 4 (VM/VMH), 10 (SCN), 2 (DM/DMH), 4 (MM/MN), 7 (MPO/PO), 1 (TM), 5 (ZI), 3 (LH) and 1 (whole hypothalamus). Standard deviations describe variation across annotations, not donor-level uncertainty. No inferential comparison was performed. All annotations originate from the same pool of 14 donors (7 AD, 7 control), so AUROCs averaged within a region are not statistically independent. MRI AUROCs and participant counts are as in b. AN and DM denote the arcuate nucleus and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (ARC and DMH in the main text).

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Fresh whole hypothalamus was obtained from eight 8-month-old female mice: four wild-type (WT) and four 5xFAD heterozygous (HET). Tissue underwent Dounce homogenization, debris cleanup and nuclei isolation. Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Chromium Controller, and 3′ gene-expression libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq platform, yielding 60,479 nuclei for analysis. b, UMAP of 60,479 nuclei, colored by major cell type: astrocytes, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, microglia, leukocytes, neurons, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and fibroblasts. c, Cross-species cell-type correspondence. Heatmap of Spearman correlations between human HypoAD cell types (columns) and mouse 5xFAD cell types (rows), with mouse cell types labeled using transferred human annotations. High diagonal values indicate concordant cell-type identities across species. d, Microglial expression of homeostatic (Csf1r, Cx3cr1, P2ry12), DAM1 (Apoe, B2m, Ctsb) and DAM2 (Axl, Itgax, Timp2) markers in four WT mice (465 nuclei) and four HET mice (912 nuclei). Violin widths show nuclear density. Embedded boxes show medians and 25th–75th percentiles, with whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Outliers are not drawn separately. Arrows indicate the direction of change in HET. Genotype effects were estimated using linear mixed models of per-nucleus expression (genotype fixed effect, random intercept for mouse, lmerTest). Two-sided t-tests used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, with Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment across nine genes. Genotype coefficients (HET − WT, 95% confidence interval) and adjusted P: Csf1r −0.36 (−0.73 to 0.01), 0.073. Cx3cr1 −0.33 (−0.60 to −0.06), 0.037. P2ry12 −0.37 (−0.65 to −0.09), 0.037. Apoe 0.62 (0.44 to 0.80), 1.3 × 10−4. B2m 0.06 (−0.08 to 0.21), 0.36. Ctsb 0.25 (0.06 to 0.43), 0.037. Axl 0.09 (0.03 to 0.16), 0.037. Itgax 0.06 (0.01 to 0.11), 0.037. Timp2 0.08 (−0.12 to 0.28), 0.37. ns, nonsignificant, *adjusted P < 0.05, ***adjusted P < 0.001. Pseudobulk edgeR results using mice as biological replicates are in Supplementary Table 16. e, Strip plot of log2 fold changes (5xFAD versus WT) for significant DEGs by cell type (pseudobulk edgeR likelihood-ratio tests, one pseudobulk per mouse, four WT and four HET mice, BH-adjusted FDR < 0.05). Each point represents one gene. Representative genes are labeled. f, Selected significantly enriched Hallmark pathways from GSEA of the 5xFAD-versus-WT comparison in astrocytes, neurons and oligodendrocytes. Fill color indicates the normalized enrichment score (NES). Gray indicates pathways not significantly enriched in that cell type. Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Yu, D. https://biorender.com/3747p8b (2026).

Jamie Gittens has withdrawn from the England Under-21 squad. He suffered an ankle injury during Tuesday’s qualifier against Kazakhstan at Molineux. The Chelsea winger left the ground on crutches. He has returned to Stamford Bridge, where the Jamie Gittens injury will now be assessed by the club’s medical staff.

Gittens picked up the knock after a challenge during the second half of England’s win over Kazakhstan. He was withdrawn as a precaution. He did not take any further part in the match. England have been careful not to overstate the issue and no further reports have come out further.

The 21-year-old struggled to put weight on the affected ankle and was seen limping around Molineux after full time. That prompted an immediate release back to his club, rather than any attempt to assess him further in camp.

According to recent reports, england Under-21 boss Lee Carsley addressed the injury directly after the game. He confirmed the nature of the knock and the decision to send Gittens home.

“Jamie got a kick on his ankle,” Carsley noted after the match. “We never take any risks. With the age of these players, we don’t ever keep them in camp to see how they are. He will go back.”.

England’s statement on the squad changes, detailed in a report from Football.London, confirmed the wider fallout from the fixture.

In a recent development, “Mukasa’s call-up follows the withdrawal of Chelsea’s Jamie Gittens and Norwich City pair Kellen Fisher and Ben Chrisene through injury,” the statement read. West Ham midfielder Divine Mukasa has been called up as cover for all three.

Gittens has been an unused substitute in every Premier League fixture Chelsea have played this season, with his only two appearances under Xabi Alonso coming in the Carabao Cup. Those minutes have offered him little platform after his substantial summer move.

Alonso’s squad selection has been a talking point since he took charge. Our earlier look at Xabi Alonso’s squad choices at Stamford Bridge covered how competitive things have become. An ankle injury will not change his pecking order in the short term. It does, though, remove any chance of him pushing his case this week.

Industry observers note that chelsea’s break has brought other headlines too. Cole Palmer also withdrew, for entirely different reasons, after his recall by senior boss Thomas Tuchel to the full England squad. Chelsea will be watching both returns closely before domestic football resumes.

Chelsea have not yet issued a formal update on the severity of the injury. Any recovery timeline will depend on an assessment by the club’s medical team once Gittens is back at Cobham. Nothing beyond the crutches seen at Molineux has been confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that given his limited game time this season, the immediate concern is less about missed fixtures than a setback to his integration under Alonso. Fans can follow how the squad shapes up before the next fixtures through our recent line-up updates. Further news on Gittens is expected once Chelsea’s medical staff finish their evaluation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:09.

Bradford City and Doncaster Rovers will square off on Saturday in a Yorkshire derby with importance at both ends of the League One table.

The hosts sit a point outside of the playoff places following a defeat last time out while their visitors have dropped into the bottom four due to consecutive losses.

Bradford City head into their first League One game of November at the weekend following an international break with the hopes of returning to winning ways and moving back into the top six.

After winning promotion from League Two and losing in the League One playoffs in the last two seasons, the Bantams picked up where they left off in early 2026-27, winning five of their first seven outings before Graham Alexander departed for Preston North End.

They then turned to Michael Duff and have struggled to continue their hot start since, winning one, drawing four and losing one of their last six league matches with the only victory coming against Stevenage in mid-October.

That did form part of a run of four straight clean sheets for the Bantams, who top the division with nine and have conceded a league-low tally of eight goals, but that came to an end in their last league outing against fellow promotion-chasers and Yorkshire rivals Huddersfield Town, who dished out a 3-0 beating at Mbanq Valley Parade.

Now, at least, on the back of a pair of confidence-boosting cup wins before their break, beating Marine 7-0 in the FA Cup and York City 4-0 in the EFL Trophy, Bradford City now sit eighth, but just two points off fourth spot, and will hope to retake a top-six spot and kickstart another hot streak in League One.

Their visitors, meanwhile, make the trip across Yorkshire in search of a return to winning ways of their own in their battle at the other end of League One.

Doncaster Rovers also won promotion from League Two in 2024-25 and finished 14th last time around on their return to the second tier but now find themselves 21st with just 12 points on the board from 13 games.

That is in no small part down to a poor away record, having lost five of seven games on the road, collected just four points and conceded 16 goals in those.

Two heavy away defeats have come consecutively for Grant McCann's side since a home victory over Sheffield Wednesday, as they lost 3-1 at Luton Town and 6-1 in their last third-tier match away at MK Dons at the end of October.

Having also since played two cup games, beating Rochdale in the EFL Trophy and losing 3-0 away at non-league Kidderminster Harriers in the FA Cup, Doncaster Rovers now head into a tough trip aiming to kickstart an upturn in form in League One and climb out of the bottom four.

Doncaster Rovers League One form:.

Doncaster Rovers form (all competitions):.

Bradford City remain without wide men Josh Neufville and Tyreik Wright, while attacker Bobby Pointon also missed their last outing through injury.

Corey O'Keeffe will continue in a wing-back role in Neufville's absence, while Antoni Sarcevic will start in midfield having served a suspension in the FA Cup for a red card received in their last league game.

George Lapslie, Adam Phillips and Nick Powell will all compete for starts in attack after Jake Beesley led the line with support from Kayden Jackson and Will Swan in the 3-0 defeat to Huddersfield.

Doncaster Rovers continue to contend with several injury concerns, as James Collins, Francis Okoronkwo, Matty Pearson, James Husband and Tommy O'Reilly should all remain sidelined.

McCann made some rotations in their two cup games and should make changes from the team that lost 6-1 to MK Dons in their last league outing, with the likes of Robbie Gotts and Will Keane pushing to start after being reduced to substitute appearances.

Hakeeb Adelakun will also challenge for a start on the wing and may join Isaac Hutchinson and Jordan Thomas in support of a lone striker unless captain and key man Owen Bailey returns to an advanced midfield role.

Bradford City possible starting lineup:.

McCracken; Pennington, Baldwin, Pratt; O'Keeffe, Sarcevic, Connolly, Touray; Swan, Beesley, Phillips.

Doncaster Rovers possible starting lineup:.

Simkin; Sterry, Grehan, Byrne, Senior; Broadbent, Gotts; Thomas, Bailey, Adelakun; Keane.

Bradford City have certainly not been at their best in League One since Michael Duff's arrival, but still boasting the league's standout defensive record, and having rebuilt confidence with a pair of dominant cup wins, we back them to come out on top at home to a struggling Doncaster team.
